item.title: Alice & Bob Reports Cat-Qubit Progress in French Quantum Computing Program
item.description:

The reported Phase 1 results—demonstrating long coherence times and error rates approaching the break‑even threshold for bosonic codes—place European efforts on a comparable footing with parallel advances at IBM, Google and academic labs pursuing surface‑code or trapped‑ion approaches. While still prototype‑level, the work signals that coordinated government funding can accelerate the transition from laboratory demonstrations to deployable quantum modules, a development that could reshape both national security computing strategies and the broader commercial supply chain.

item.description:

By coupling AI‑driven experiment design with atom‑by‑atom control, the company could accelerate calibration cycles and reduce the overhead traditionally associated with neutral‑atom error correction. If successful, the effort would diversify the global hardware ecosystem beyond U.S. and European players and give industry a new candidate for scalable quantum advantage, though achieving true logical qubits at that size still faces steep coherence and connectivity challenges.

FlipFlop Tuoyuan, a Chinese quantum hardware startup, has secured over $14 million in early-stage funding to develop neutral-atom quantum processing units. item.title: UK Government and UKRI Unveil £78M ($103.8M USD) Quantum Commercialization, Networking, and Skills Package
item.description:
Curator's Take: This £78 million package marks the UK’s most ambitious push yet to turn quantum research into market‑ready products, signaling that policymakers see commercial sensing and networking as the next revenue streams after qubit hardware breakthroughs. By coupling funding for supply‑chain firms with a boost to the QuEST Apprentices Programme and an extra £17 million for AI‑HPC integration, the initiative dovetails with recent European and US efforts to build end‑to‑end quantum ecosystems rather than isolated labs. If the grants succeed in delivering scalable sensors or secure communication links, UK companies could capture early market share in sectors such as telecom, aerospace and health tech; however, the true impact will hinge on how quickly industry partners can translate prototype performance into reliable, manufacturable devices.

The UK government and UK Research and Innovation (UKRI) have announced a £78 million (approximately $103.8 million USD) funding package to advance quantum sensing, networking, and workforce development. This initiative, part of the National Quantum Strategy, includes grants for commercial applications, supply-chain development, and an expansion of the QuEST Apprentices Programme. An additional £17 million has been allocated for integrating AI and high-performance computing with quantum platforms, aiming to solidify the UK's global leadership in quantum technologies. item.title: NVIDIA and Jülich Run 104-Qubit Magic State Cultivation Simulation on JUPITER Supercomputer
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that Europe’s first exascale machine can realistically model a full‑scale fault‑tolerant protocol, confirming that magic‑state cultivation could slash the qubit count needed for error‑corrected computation. By demonstrating a 104‑qubit simulation on JUPITER’s GH200 GPUs, NVIDIA and Jülich bridge the gap between theoretical overhead estimates and practical hardware requirements, echoing recent advances in surface‑code benchmarking and resource‑reduction techniques. The result gives architects a concrete data point for designing near‑term quantum processors with far fewer physical qubits than previously thought, though the findings still rely on idealized noise models that must be validated on actual devices.

NVIDIA and Jülich Supercomputing Centre simulated a 104-qubit fault-tolerant quantum computing experiment on the JUPITER supercomputer, Europe's first exascale system. This simulation, detailed in an NVIDIA technical report, validated a magic state cultivation protocol that significantly reduces physical qubit overhead. The project utilized JUPITER's 8,192 NVIDIA GH200 Grace Hopper Superchips and advanced software to model complex quantum error correction. item.title: Quantinuum Demonstrates 99.9995% Logical Memory Fidelity on Helios Trapped-Ion Processor
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article marks a concrete step toward fault‑tolerant quantum computing by showing that Quantinuum’s Helios trapped‑ion processor can store quantum information with a logical fidelity of 99.9995 %, corresponding to a per‑round error rate of just 5 × 10⁻⁶ on a distance‑7 surface code. The exponential suppression factor of 12 demonstrates that scaling the code distance continues to yield dramatic improvements, echoing recent advances from superconducting platforms and confirming that trapped ions can meet the stringent thresholds required for large‑scale architectures such as Quantinuum’s upcoming Apollo system. For practitioners, the result suggests that logical memory—once a major bottleneck—may soon be reliable enough to support deeper algorithms without overwhelming overhead, though extending this performance to full logical gates and multi‑qubit operations remains an open challenge.

Quantinuum has demonstrated a 99.9995% logical memory fidelity on its Helios trapped-ion quantum computer, achieving a logical error rate of 5 × 10-6 per syndrome-extraction round on a distance-7 code. This performance shows exponential error suppression with increasing code distance, with a suppression factor of 12. These results align with the performance targets for Quantinuum's future universal fault-tolerant quantum system, Apollo. By meeting the error‑correction benchmark in a compact, CMOS‑compatible platform, the work builds on recent advances from Intel and other groups that have pushed individual silicon qubit fidelities toward the same level, bringing scalable, chip‑integrated quantum hardware closer to reality. The result is promising for larger arrays, though extending the technique beyond five qubits and integrating full error‑correcting codes will be the next critical challenges.

Researchers at RIKEN and collaborators have achieved high-fidelity simultaneous control of five silicon spin qubits, maintaining over 99.9% accuracy. They overcame crosstalk caused by AC-Stark shifts through a new calibration protocol, enabling the use of a single microwave control line. This breakthrough meets the fault-tolerant threshold for quantum error correction and paves the way for more scalable quantum computers. By marrying analog annealing with digital control pulses, the work expands the toolbox for programmable condensed‑matter simulators and puts D‑Wave’s platform in direct competition with gate‑model approaches that are still limited to far smaller lattices. The result hints at faster exploration of exotic materials, though it remains confined to Hamiltonians that map naturally onto the annealer’s connectivity and noise profile.

D-Wave has successfully demonstrated 3D analog-digital quantum simulation of higher-order topological insulators using up to 728 qubits on an Advantage2 superconducting quantum annealing processor. This achievement, detailed in a research study on arXiv, involved new analog-digital quantum control protocols to measure localized boundary modes and extract 3D bulk topological invariants. This breakthrough confirms the utility of analog-digital quantum annealing hardware as a programmable simulator for condensed matter physics and topological materials. item.title: Demonstration of Logical Error Suppression in a Surface Code Memory on a Cloud-Accessible IBM Superconducting Processor
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article marks one of the first demonstrations that a surface‑code memory can be run on a publicly accessible superconducting processor with measurable logical error suppression, showing that careful circuit compilation—short readout, fused measurement/reset and an XX echo—can cut per‑round logical errors by up to fourfold. By comparing distance‑3 and distance‑6 layouts on the same hardware, the authors provide concrete evidence that increasing code distance still yields a tangible reduction in logical error rates (≈ 0.5% → 0.2%) even amid realistic qubit‑to‑qubit variation and correlated noise. The work bridges the gap between laboratory‑scale error‑correction experiments and cloud‑based quantum services, suggesting that scalable fault tolerance may be achievable without bespoke hardware upgrades, though long‑lived error correlations remain a key obstacle to be tamed.

Quantum error correction can suppress logical errors exponentially with code distance when physical noise is below threshold. Realizing this on hardware requires tight coordination among quantum gates, mid-circuit measurements, and qubit coherence. Device variation, noise asymmetry, and correlations across space and time complicate the translation of these capabilities into logical error suppression. Here, we study rotated surface-code memory on an IBM Nighthawk r2 processor. Performance varies across tested processor placements, which we attribute to differences in qubit quality. We optimize the code by combining short readout, fused measurement and reset, and an XX echo on data qubits during ancilla readout. Compared with standard readout without reset or echo, the optimized syndrome extraction circuit reduces the median per-round logical error rate by factors of 3.8 in the X basis and 1.4 in the Z basis. In memory experiments of up to 150 rounds, the distance advantage weakens, alongside long-lived correlations that may reflect a persistent error component. Under our optimization recipe, increasing the protected distance from 3 to 6 while holding the other distance fixed reduces the per-round logical error rate from 0.53% to 0.24% in Z memory and from 0.52% to 0.22% in X memory. The corresponding error-suppression factors under maximum-likelihood decoding are 1.68 and 1.85. These results connect circuit compilation and optimization to surface-code memory performance and limitations, and motivate QPU and QEC circuit codesign for fault-tolerant quantum computing primitives on current cloud hardware.

item.title: Quality-of-Transmission Estimation in Quantum Networks: Compute, Simulate, or Learn?
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article tackles a bottleneck for future quantum internets by asking how network controllers can quickly gauge the fidelity of entanglement across candidate paths—a metric essential for routing, scheduling and memory management. By adapting the optical‑network quality‑of‑transmission mindset into a compute/simulate/learn framework, it shows that analytical formulas suffice only in trivial regimes, full‑scale simulators are needed when stochastic memory effects dominate, and compact machine‑learning surrogates can deliver near‑real‑time estimates once trained. The work links directly to the growing body of research on quantum network control planes and suggests a practical path toward scalable, low‑latency resource allocation, while warning that data‑generation costs and sim‑to‑real transfer remain open challenges.

Future quantum networks will rely on control-plane decisions such as routing, scheduling, entanglement provisioning, purification, and memory allocation. Each decision depends on a timely and reliable estimate of the quality of the entanglement that a candidate path can deliver, with end-to-end fidelity as a central metric. Inspired by the optical-networking experience with quality-of-transmission (QoT) estimation, this article asks when a quantum controller should compute fidelity analytically, simulate it, or learn a surrogate model. The optical analogy is useful but incomplete: optical QoT estimation often predicts a scalar transmission margin, whereas quantum QoT estimation must account for probabilistic entanglement generation, random memory waiting times, decoherence, state consumption, and measurement constraints that can make fidelity a stochastic target. We propose a compute/simulate/learn framework for quantum QoT estimation and illustrate it with a simulation-based proof of concept. Our study shows that analytical composition can be sufficient in simple regimes, that simulation becomes necessary when stochastic memory effects shape the delivered fidelity distribution, and that lightweight learned surrogates can approximate simulator labels at much lower runtime cost for online control. We close with open challenges for deployment, including stochastic targets, sim-to-real transfer, data-generation cost, physics-informed learning, and generalization beyond individual paths to full network topologies.

item.title: Improving the estimation of spin-bath parameters via initial correlations and a two-qubit probe
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that a modest two‑qubit probe—when the second qubit is prepared in a correlated state with the environment—can boost spin‑bath parameter estimation by up to an order of magnitude compared with conventional single‑qubit sensing. By exploiting initial system‑environment correlations rather than direct inter‑qubit coupling, the authors achieve a factor‑3–4 improvement in quantum Fisher information for coupling strength and about eightfold for temperature, highlighting a practical route to more precise noise spectroscopy on solid‑state platforms. The result dovetails with recent interest in correlated probes for quantum metrology, though its impact will depend on experimental ability to engineer and preserve those initial correlations in realistic hardware.

We study how a second qubit can improve the estimation of spin-environment parameters when only one of the two qubits is measured. Both qubits are coupled to a common spin bath through the exactly solvable central-spin model, in which populations and coherences both evolve. Because the bath operator coupled to the qubits commutes with the bath Hamiltonian, the environment induces no effective interaction between the qubits. Without initial correlations or direct inter-qubit coupling, the two-qubit probe therefore performs exactly like a single qubit. When initial system-environment correlations are included, preparing the second qubit reshapes the environment statistics in a parameter-dependent way, and the measured qubit reads out this imprint. This improves the quantum Fisher information (QFI) for the coupling strength by factors of 3-4 relative to a correlated single-qubit probe, and by more than an order of magnitude relative to an uncorrelated one. For temperature estimation, the improvement reaches a factor of about 8. A direct Ising coupling does not help by itself, but the advantage persists in its presence. We also derive the classical Fisher information for arbitrary projective measurements and identify the measurement that saturates the QFI, which in general lies out of the equatorial plane of the Bloch sphere.

item.title: Solving Large-Scale Parameter Inference in Controllable Nuclear Fusion via Coherent Ising Machines and Block Coordinate Descent
item.description:

Bayesian inference enables self-consistent plasma parameter inversion in tokamak integrated data analysis by fusing multi-source diagnostics. However, under nonlinear Gaussian likelihoods, finding the maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimate typically relies on sampling methods whose high computational overhead precludes real-time plasma control. To address this bottleneck, we propose a Bayesian inversion framework using a Coherent Ising Machine (CIM)-a quantum computing architecture based on coupled degenerate optical parametric oscillators (DOPOs). With native all-to-all connectivity, the CIM directly maps the negative log-posterior potential onto a spin Hamiltonian and leverages quantum vacuum fluctuations for rapid state-space search during pitchfork bifurcation. Validated on plasma current profile inversion for the EAST tokamak, this method achieves a single-run solution time of approximately 1 ms. Although current qubit limits necessitate a block-wise iterative scheme that prevents full real-time execution today, rapidly scaling quantum hardware offers a clear pathway toward real-time tokamak control.

item.title: ConQUESTA: Topology-Aware Post-Training Structural Pruning of Quantum Neural Networks
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article introduces ConQUESTA, a topology‑aware post‑training pruning framework that jointly optimizes task saliency and compiler cost to trim entangling gates in quantum neural networks while guaranteeing an accuracy bound. By evaluating whole‑circuit masks across multiple coupling maps, the method achieves up to 82 % reduction in two‑qubit operations on standard benchmarks—far surpassing simple baseline pruning and dramatically easing the gate‑depth constraints of near‑term hardware. The work signals a practical step toward scalable QNN deployment on sparse superconducting or ion‑trap devices, though its current validation is limited to small (4–12 qubit) models and a handful of datasets.

Deploying quantum neural networks (QNNs) on sparse hardware requires preserving task accuracy while reducing compiler-induced two-qubit gates, SWAPs, and depth. We present ConQUESTA (\underline{C}onstrained \underline{Qu}antum \underline{E}ntangler \underline{S}election with \underline{T}opology \underline{A}wareness), a post training pruning framework that combines task saliency with compiler cost, screens candidate entanglers, and searches complete pruning masks under an explicit accuracy constraint. Unlike one-shot ranking, each mask is transpiled as a whole across multiple coupling topologies. Across 4-, 6-, and 8-qubit QNNs and eight model seeds at 55% pruning, ConQUESTA achieves mean resource reductions of 61.6% on Breast Cancer, 72.0% on Digits01, and 82.2% on Iris, exceeding the strongest matched simple baseline by 3.5, 1.7, and 8.9 percentage points, respectively. Fixed-mask recovery raises feasibility from 16/24 to 22/24 runs. In a fixed-k=4 scaling study on a scaling probe of 4 to 12-qubits, the raw mask space grew from 495 to 12.1M while the evaluated masks increase only from 189 to 305. Resource-weight changes alter depth/routing priorities with at most a 0.44-point mean validation shift.

item.title: SpinControl: Control Software for Prototyping and Benchmarking of Spin-Qubit Devices and Measurement Protocols
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article introduces SpinControl, a purpose‑built control stack that finally bridges the gap between low‑level hardware tuning and high‑level circuit programming for spin‑qubit processors. By cleanly separating data from behavior, modularizing functionality, and embedding CI‑driven robustness, it lets experimental teams prototype new pulse sequences or calibration routines while giving algorithm developers a stable API for running circuits—something that has been missing as silicon‑based qubits scale beyond a handful of dots. The framework’s cloud connectivity, virtual‑gate compilation and spin‑qubit‑specific GUIs could accelerate both device optimization and benchmark reproducibility across labs, positioning spin qubits to compete more directly with superconducting platforms. However, its impact will depend on community adoption and integration with existing hardware stacks, which remain fragmented today.

Quantum computers require software to control the states of the qubits. As the actions on qubits grow in complexity with circuit execution, calibration, and benchmarking, the complexity of the control software grows in tandem. Spin-qubit quantum computers are at a stage where experimentalists need low-level access for tuning and calibration, and quantum algorithm researchers want high-level circuit-level access. In this article, we present the software design of SpinControl. SpinControl integrates three architectural metrics: 1) customizability, to allow prototyping devices and measurement protocols, is achieved by separating data and behaviour; 2) modularity and extensibility are achieved by separating functionalities into different components; and 3) robustness, to reliably execute quantum circuits on many qubits, is achieved by CI pipelines and input validation. SpinControl allows different types of measurements while customizing the instruments used, the pulse or circuit program executed, and the data processing. It allows building standardized experiments from measurement and analysis building blocks and executing these for calibration in a custom and conditional order. SpinControl implements these functionalities alongside robust configuration and data management, a connection to the cloud, and calibration scheduling. Pulse and circuit compilation, virtual gate matrices, as well as spin-qubit-specific GUIs integrated by SpinControl, make heavy use of software packages developed by Delft University of Technology: pulse lib, core-tools (both open source), and QConstruct

item.title: Learning angles for quantum approximate optimization
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article tackles one of QAOA’s biggest practical hurdles—finding high‑quality variational angles—by training a neural model that predicts them directly from the problem graph, turning an expensive per‑instance optimizer into a single forward pass. The approach not only matches solver performance on current quantum hardware but also generalizes to unseen topologies such as Barabási‑Albert and 2D grids, suggesting a scalable route for real‑world combinatorial workloads. By amortizing the data‑generation cost, the method could make QAOA viable for industrial settings where many similar optimization instances must be solved repeatedly.

The Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) and its variants are leading algorithms to help solve challenging combinatorial optimization problems. QAOA maps these problems to Ising Hamiltonians such that their ground state is the desired solution. Candidate solutions are then drawn from a variational quantum circuit. The performance of QAOA hinges on a set of variational angles. However, finding good angles is an instance-specific and computationally expensive non-convex classical optimization task. Here, we learn the mapping from the problem instance to high-quality QAOA angles. Our learned models replace the per-instance optimization, that we call the solver, with a single forward pass that is several orders of magnitude faster than the solver with a near identical quality. Our models further generalize to unseen topologies such as Barabási-Albert and 2D grid graphs. Experiments on quantum hardware confirm that QAOA samples with angles produced by our open-source models are indistinguishable from solver angles. Crucially, models sensitive to the topology of the problem instance increase the quality of the QAOA angles. Our work amortizes a major bottleneck in QAOA by an up-front data generation and training cost. Importantly, this cost can be amortized over time in settings where many similar problems are optimized on a regular basis, as is often the case in applications for industry.

item.title: Exponential-SWAP gate between bosonic motional modes of trapped ions
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article demonstrates the first experimental realization of a continuously tunable exponential‑SWAP gate between two bosonic motional modes of trapped ions, providing a genuine hybrid interaction that can interpolate smoothly between doing nothing and swapping entire quantum states. By leveraging both spin‑independent and spin‑dependent beam‑splitter couplings, the work extends the toolbox for bosonic encoding schemes—such as cat or GKP qubits—that have so far been dominated by superconducting cavity platforms, opening new routes to error‑corrected logical operations and entanglement generation in ion traps. The exponential-SWAP (eSWAP) gate generates a coherent superposition of identity and SWAP operations, with continuously tunable amplitudes. We experimentally implement this gate between two bosonic motional modes of trapped ions using spin-independent and spin-dependent beam splitter interactions. Measurements of selected slices of the joint characteristic function for distinct input states test the gate and demonstrate continuous control of the identity-SWAP superposition. This implementation provides a tunable interaction for hybrid qubit-bosonic quantum information processing.

By coupling MD, DFT and wavefunction methods across CPUs, GPUs and a 54‑qubit IQM QPU, the authors demonstrate a practical hybrid workflow that could accelerate studies of membrane proteins and drug targets where subtle electronic effects matter. The work builds on recent efforts to embed QPUs in HPC pipelines, but it also highlights current limits such as modest qubit counts and error mitigation requirements before routine quantum‑accelerated biomolecular modeling becomes commonplace.

Predicting chemical reactions in biomolecules is challenging because reactive centers are embedded within complex environments that strongly influence their energetics and mechanisms. Here, we present a hybrid quantum-classical workflow that combines molecular dynamics, density functional theory, and correlated wavefunction methods, tightly integrating CPUs, GPUs, and quantum processing units (QPUs) to enable simulations across multiple length and accuracy scales. We apply this approach to ADGRG1 autoproteolysis, a maturation reaction in an adhesion G protein-coupled receptor that has not previously been studied using correlated electronic-structure methods. Our simulations treat a biologically realistic system containing more than one million atoms, including the full-length uncleaved receptor embedded in an endoplasmic-reticulum membrane, while incorporating a 54-qubit IQM quantum processor and up to 1,200 NVIDIA H100 GPUs. These results demonstrate how quantum computers can serve as accelerators within scalable scientific workflows, extending correlated electronic-structure methods to biologically relevant systems.

item.title: Concrete Functions in Private Simultaneous Quantum Messages: Quantum Advantages and Structural Limitations
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article demonstrates that even in the ultra‑minimal private simultaneous quantum messages model, entanglement can cut communication costs for concrete total functions such as three‑party equality and majority well below classical lower bounds, highlighting a genuine quantum advantage with only a handful of qubits. At the same time it uncovers sharp structural limits—most notably the impossibility of a perfectly correct and private protocol for three‑bit AND using just one shared three‑qubit state—showing that not every function benefits from the same shortcut. By pinpointing exactly where entanglement helps and where higher‑dimensional resources are required, the work bridges recent advances in quantum communication complexity with practical considerations for near‑term hardware implementations of secure multiparty protocols.

Private simultaneous quantum messages (PSQM) provide a minimal model of noninteractive secure multiparty quantum computation, yet their communication complexity for concrete functions remains poorly understood. We show that familiar total functions already exhibit both genuine quantum advantages and strong structural limitations. For three-party equality on $n$-bit inputs, which determines whether the players' $n$-bit strings are identical, we construct an entanglement-assisted protocol with asymptotic communication $(1.633\ldots)n$ qubits, whereas every perfectly correct protocol without prior entanglement requires at least $3n$ qubits. For three-bit majority, one shared GHZ state and one transmitted qubit per player suffice for perfect correctness and perfect privacy, reducing the communication from the optimal classical cost of six bits to three qubits. Three-bit AND behaves differently. No perfectly correct and perfectly private protocol exists when the players share an arbitrary three-qubit state, apply arbitrary local unitary encodings, and transmit one qubit each. However, increasing the local dimension overcomes this obstruction: one shared three-qutrit GHZ state and one transmitted qutrit per player yield a one-shot protocol with total communication $3\log_2 3$. Together with the six-bit classical lower bound, this gives a strict quantum communication advantage. More generally, for every $k\geq 3$, we construct a perfectly correct and perfectly private one-shot protocol for $k$-bit AND using one qudit of dimension at most $k$ per player, and hence at most $k\log_2 k$ qubits in total.

item.title: Quantum approximate stochastic combinatorial optimisation
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article tackles a notoriously hard class of problems—two‑stage stochastic combinatorial optimisation—by embedding the scenario‑dependent recourse directly into a variational quantum‑walk circuit, allowing the algorithm to search over first‑stage decisions without explicitly computing costly expected minima. By demonstrating that QASCO concentrates probability on optimal choices more effectively than earlier two‑stage QAOA approaches and can be calibrated with a depth‑independent parameter set that generalises to unseen instances of size beyond 2³², it points toward scalable quantum heuristics for real‑world planning under uncertainty. However, the results are still limited to exact state‑vector simulations, so experimental validation on near‑term hardware will be the next crucial step.

Two-stage stochastic combinatorial optimisation concerns discrete decisions made before all relevant information is known. An initial decision is made; once uncertainty is resolved, it can be adapted to the realised scenario, at a cost. The aim is to find the initial decision that minimises the upfront cost plus the expected cost of optimal adaptation. The first-stage decision problem is often NP-hard, and computing the expected minimum recourse cost can be $\#\mathrm{P}$-hard for a single first-stage candidate. We introduce Quantum Approximate Stochastic Combinatorial Optimisation (QASCO), a variational quantum-walk ansatz that coherently incorporates scenario-dependent recourse into its dynamics to search over first-stage decisions without explicitly evaluating expected minimum recourse costs. We demonstrate QASCO for MaxCut with stochastic edge weights, obtain a circuit with polynomial per-layer gate complexity, and study the ansatz via exact state-vector simulation. Across the instances considered, QASCO concentrates amplitude more effectively on stochastic-optimal first-stage decisions than a previously proposed two-stage QAOA construction. We further show that the ansatz can be calibrated using a depth-independent number of parameters and applied to unseen instances without further circuit-parameter optimisation, including joint decision--scenario--recourse spaces spanning more than $2^{32}$ configurations. Under a query-cost model, comparison with the tested classical heuristics using sample-average approximations of the expected minimum recourse cost shows that QASCO more reliably reaches globally optimal first-stage solutions while requiring fewer cut evaluations. These results show how to incorporate scenario-dependent recourse into the ansatz dynamics, providing a general framework for variational quantum walks in two-stage stochastic combinatorial optimisation.

item.title: Discovering state-of-the-art quantum circuits with large language models
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that large language models can act as creative partners in quantum circuit design, automatically generating reversible architectures that beat the best hand‑crafted solutions on most benchmark tasks. By coupling an LLM proposer with a rigorous evaluator, the authors demonstrate a scalable way to explore the vast space of Toffoli‑efficient circuits—a bottleneck that has limited practical algorithm deployment on near‑term hardware. The approach could accelerate the discovery of low‑overhead primitives for chemistry, optimization and number‑theoretic applications, though its success still depends on high‑quality evaluation metrics and may require further tuning to handle larger, more complex problems.

Significant efforts are currently being directed toward the implementation of large-scale quantum information processors, but realizing useful quantum advantage also requires the development of efficient quantum algorithms. While for many practical problems the dominant resource costs are associated with a small set of computational primitives, optimizing them in the quantum setting presents unique challenges, including a reversibility constraint absent from ordinary classical computation. Here we introduce an evolutionary framework in which large language models (LLMs) propose circuit designs and an independent evaluator verifies and scores them. We apply this framework to tasks spanning numerical computation, chemistry, optimization, quantum simulation, and number theory. In seven of the eight tasks, the discovered circuits significantly reduce both Toffoli and qubit counts relative to the state of the art. In the eighth, the search discovers a new reversible architecture for prime-field modular inversion. By handling reversibility differently, the architecture makes divsteps -- a classical algorithm previously impractical for reversible integer arithmetic -- viable and substantially improves the Toffoli-qubit trade-off for modular inversion. These results open the door for evaluator-guided LLM co-design of new algorithmic structures for quantum computation.

item.title: SynDebug: A Framework to Debug Logic Bugs in Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computing Programs
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article marks the first demonstration of a systems‑level debugging framework that works inside encoded fault‑tolerant quantum programs, filling a glaring gap left by earlier tools that only inspected logical circuits. By embedding lightweight assertion primitives directly into surface‑code–style QEC layers with an average depth penalty of just 1.8 % and no detectable rise in logical error rates, SynDebug makes it feasible to catch logic bugs before they explode into costly runtime failures—a crucial step as experimental groups move from small prototypes toward scalable FTQC architectures. The work dovetails with recent advances in real‑time syndrome processing and could accelerate the development cycle for large‑scale algorithms such as Shor’s or quantum chemistry, though its current validation is largely simulation‑based and will need hardware trials to confirm performance under realistic noise.

Fault-tolerant quantum computing (FTQC) introduces substantial systems-level complexity through quantum error correction (QEC), making debugging FTQC programs challenging. Existing quantum debugging approaches primarily target logical-level circuits and do not naturally support debugging within realistic FTQC execution flows. We present SynDebug, the first systems-level debugging framework for FTQC programs. SynDebug introduces lightweight assertion-based debugging primitives that operate directly within encoded FTQC infrastructures while avoiding additional logical surface area and minimizing temporal overhead. We evaluate SynDebug across multiple QEC code families, code distances, and encoded workloads, including state preparation, entanglement validation, and Shor-style programs. Our results demonstrate that SynDebug enables practical FTQC debugging with an average 1.8% additional circuit depth overhead (0% in most cases) and no measurable increase in the logical error rate, showing that systems-level debugging for large-scale FTQC applications is both feasible and practical.

ORCA Computing has launched its PT-3 photonic quantum system in London, integrating it with NVIDIA GPU-accelerated computing infrastructure.
